description.en-US: The settings_schema this record was built from. It is what the read path follows to find the field definition for this setting name, including the declared allow_override that applies until a tenant admin overrides it on the row.
Copied from the schema at creation. Denormalized deliberately: the unique key and every read filter are keyed on it, and joining settings_schemas for each would cost a join per setting item.

Copied from the schema at creation. It says which kind of owner the setting is *for*, which is not always the owner it is stored against: a tenant admin's own row for a user-level setting has level=user, owner_type=tenant.
What kind of thing owns this row. The fan-out selects children by owner_type, so it is the column that separates a tenant's own record from the org and user records it enforces onto.

The id of the owning tenant, organization or user. Not a foreign key: settings must never reference iam tables, because iam already depends on settings and the reverse edge would be a startup-aborting cycle.

The setting name, matching a field in the registered schema. Unique within a module across all of its levels, so a module cannot declare the same name at two levels and leave a read ambiguous. Immutable: renaming would strand the value under a name no schema declares.
The stored value, always wrapped as {"value": <value>}. The envelope exists because json_map has no array form, so a scalar and a list both need an object around them to share one column.

Whether an owner below the tenant may keep their own value for this setting. Per-record rather than schema metadata, so a tenant admin decides it per tenant instead of a module fixing it for everyone at build time. Only a tenant owner may write it: it is the mechanism that locks the levels below, so an org or user setting it would be escalating their own privilege. Null on a row no tenant admin has ruled on, which reads as overridable -- the restrictive default would silently lock every setting nobody has considered.
